can someone tell me what the equivalent of tf.keras.Input() in pytorch is?

At the documentation it says, "Initiates a Keras Tensor", so does it just creates a new empty tensor?

Thanks

There's no equivalent in PyTorch to the Keras' Input. All you have to do is pass on the inputs as a tensor to the PyTorch model.

For eg: If you're working with a Conv net:


# Keras Code
input_image = Input(shape=(32,32,3)) # An input image of 32x32x3 (HxWxC)
feature = Conv2D(16, activation='relu', kernel_size=(3, 3))(input_image)

# PyTorch code
input_tensor = torch.randn(1, 3, 32, 32) # An input tensor of shape BatchSizexChannelsxHeightxWidth
feature = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=16, kernel_size=(2, 2))(input_tensor)

If it is a normal Dense layer:

# Keras
dense_input = Input(shape=(1,))
features = Dense(100)(dense_input)

# PyTorch
input_tensor = torch.tensor([10]) # A 1x1 tensor with value 10
features = nn.Linear(1, 100)(input_tensor)

The `tf.keras.Input` function is used to create an input layer for a model.
It returns a symbolic tensor (the same type as the output of other layers).
This allows you to specify how your inputs will be processed,
before defining the model itself.

```
import tensorflow as tf

# Define an input layer and specify shape
input_layer = tf.keras.Input(shape=(32,))

# Define a hidden layer and specify activation function
hidden_layer = tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='relu')(input_layer)

# Define output layer and specify activation function
output_layer = tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax')(hidden_layer)
```

In this example, we define an input layer with 32 features, a hidden layer with 10 neurons and ReLU activation function, and an output layer with 10 neurons and softmax activation function.

Note that the `Input` function doesn't actually create any variables or do anything else – it just specifies the shape and data type of the input data that expects your model to get. The actual computation happens in the subsequent layers.

For more information see [TensorFlow's official documentation](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/keras/sequential_model).

```

Note 

As all the other losses in PyTorch, this function expects the first argument, `input`  , to be the output of the model (e.g. the neural network)
and the second, `target`  , to be the observations in the dataset.

### Use nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel instead of multiprocessing or nn.DataParallel 

Most use cases involving batched inputs and multiple GPUs should default to
using [`DistributedDataParallel`](../generated/torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel.html#torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel "torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel")  to utilize more
than one GPU. 

There are significant caveats to using CUDA models with [`multiprocessing`](../multiprocessing.html#module-torch.multiprocessing "torch.multiprocessing")  ; unless care is taken to meet the data handling
requirements exactly, it is likely that your program will have incorrect or
undefined behavior.

I am working on implementing a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) in PyTorch 1.5.0.

For computing the loss of the generator, I compute both the negative probabilities that the discriminator mis-classifies an all-real minibatch and an all-(generator-generated-)fake minibatch. Then, I back-propagate both parts sequentially and finally apply the step function.

Calculating and back-propagating the part of the loss which is a function of the mis-classifications of the generated fake data seems straight forward, since during back-propagation of that loss term, the backward path leads through the generator who has produced the fake data in the first place.

However, classification of all-real-data minibatches does not involve passing data through the generator. Therefore, I was wondering whether the following code snipped would still calculate gradients for the generator or whether it would not calculate any gradients at all (since the backward path does not lead through the generator and the discriminator is in eval-mode while updating the generator)?

# Update generator #
net.generator.train()
net.discriminator.eval()
net.generator.zero_grad()

# All-real minibatch
x_real = get_all_real_minibatch()
y_true = torch.full((batch_size,), label_fake).long()  # Pretend true targets were fake
y_pred = net.discriminator(x_real)  # Produces softmax probability distribution over (0=label_fake,1=label_real)

loss_real = NLLLoss(torch.log(y_pred), y_true) 
loss_real.backward()
optimizer_generator.step()

If this doesn’t work as intended, how could I make it work? Thanks in advance!

No gradients are propagated to the generator, as no calculation was performed with any of the generator's parameters. The discriminator being in eval mode would not prevent the gradients from propagating to the generator, albeit they would be slightly different if you are using layers that behave differently in eval mode compared to train mode, such as dropout.

The misclassification of real images is not part of training the generator, because it doesn't gain anything from this information. Conceptually, what should the generator learn from the fact that the discriminator failed to correctly classify a real image? The sole task of the generator is to create a fake image such that the discriminator thinks it's real, therefore the only relevant information for the generator is whether the discriminator was able to identify the fake image. If the discriminator was indeed able to identify the fake image, the generator needs to adjust itself to create a more convincing fake.

Of course it's not a binary case, but the generator always tries to improve the fake image such that the discriminator is even more convinced that it was a real image. The generator's goal is not to make the discriminator be doubtful (probability of 0.5 that it's real or fake), but that the discriminator is fully convinced that it's real, even though it's fake. That's why they are adversarial, not cooperative.

The generator will be updated by this code.

In your case, you have two losses: `loss_fake` and `loss_real`. You want to update the generator based on these two losses. The generator is only used to generate fake images, so we can ignore the real image part. We just need to know that the generator is being used to generate fake images.

So, let's say we have some fake images `G(z)` and their labels `label_fake`, then we can write:

```
z = torch.randn(batch_size, z_dim)
fake_images = G(z)
loss_fake = criterion(D(fake_images), label_fake)
loss_fake.backward(retain_graph=True)
```

Here, `retain_graph=True` means that we want to keep the graph alive after the backward pass. This is because we want to use the same graph to compute the gradient of the generator.

Now, we can update the generator using the optimizer:

```
optimizer_G.step()

This will update the generator based on the gradients computed in the previous step.

### Fake Implementations of PyTorch Operators 

Recall that during tracing, we are executing the program with [fake Tensors](https://localhost:8000/docs/main/torch.compiler_fake_tensor.html)  ,
which have no data. In general we cannot call the actual implementations of
PyTorch operators with fake Tensors. Thus each operator needs to have an
additional fake (a.k.a. “meta”) implementation, which inputs and outputs fake
Tensors, that matches the behavior of the actual implementation in terms of
shapes and other forms of metadata carried by fake Tensors. 

For example, note how the fake implementation of [`torch.index_select()`](generated/torch.index_select.html#torch.index_select "torch.index_select")  computes the shape of the output using the shape of the input (while ignoring
input data and returning empty output data). 

```
def meta_index_select(self, dim, index):
    result_size = list(self.size())
    if self.dim() > 0:
        result_size[dim] = index.numel()
    return self.new_empty(result_size)

```

### Division by Zero in Autograd 

When performing division by zero in PyTorch (e.g., `x / 0`  ), the forward pass will produce `inf`  values following IEEE-754 floating point arithmetic. While these `inf`  values can be masked out before computing the final loss (e.g., via indexing or masking), the autograd system still tracks and differentiates through the full computation graph, including the division by zero operation. 

During backpropagation, this can lead to problematic gradient expressions. For example: 

```
x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

y = x / div          # Results in [inf, 1]
mask = div != 0      # [False, True]
loss = y[mask].sum()
loss.backward()
print(x.grad)        # [nan, 1], not [0, 1]

```

In this example, even though we only use the masked output (which excludes the division by zero), autograd still computes gradients through the full computation graph, including the division by zero operation. This results in `nan`  gradients for the masked elements, which can cause training instability. 

To avoid this issue, there are several recommended approaches: 

1. Mask before division:

```
x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

mask = div != 0
safe = torch.zeros_like(x)
safe[mask] = x[mask] / div[mask]
loss = safe.sum()
loss.backward()      # Produces safe gradients [0, 1]

```

2. Use MaskedTensor (experimental API):

```
from torch.masked import as_masked_tensor

x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

What is the difference between copying a tensor using torch.tensor(sourcetensor) and tensor.clone().detach()?

Like torch.tensor(srctsr) always copies data, tensor.clone().detach() copies data too.

x = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])
y1 = x.clone().detach()
y2 = torch.tensor(x)
x[0] = 0
print(y1, y2) # both are same

So they seem to be exactly the same. Below is the explanation given in the PyTorch documentation about torch.tensor() and torch.clone().detach()

Therefore torch.tensor(x) is equivalent to x.clone().detach() and torch.tensor(x, requires_grad=True) is equivalent to x.clone().detach().requires_grad_(True). The equivalents using clone() and detach() are recommended.

So if they are equivalent to each other, why is .clone().detach() more preferred than the other?

The difference is described here. I am adding some text (from the link) for the sake of completeness.

  • torch.tensor() always copies data. If you have a Tensor data and want to avoid a copy, use torch.Tensor.requires_grad_() or torch.Tensor.detach().

  • When data is a tensor x, torch.tensor() reads out ‘the data’ from whatever it is passed, and constructs a leaf variable. Therefore torch.tensor(x) is equivalent to x.clone().detach() and torch.tensor(x, requires_grad=True) is equivalent to x.clone().detach().requires_grad_(True). The equivalents using clone() and detach() are recommended.

The main difference is that `torch.tensor` will copy the input tensor's data by default (unless you pass `share_memory=True`). On the other hand, `.clone()` does not copy the data unless you pass `non_blocking=True`. This means that `.clone()` can be faster when cloning tensors on GPU.

In general, it's better to use `.clone()` instead of `torch.tensor`, because:

* It doesn't require an extra memory allocation for the new tensor.
* It doesn't have to check whether the input tensor is already a tensor or not.
* It has less overhead overall.

See [this GitHub issue](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/67549#issuecomment-898639629) for more details.

torch.reshape 
==============================================================

torch. reshape ( *input*  , *shape* ) → [Tensor](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor") 
:   Returns a tensor with the same data and number of elements as `input`  ,
but with the specified shape. When possible, the returned tensor will be a view
of `input`  . Otherwise, it will be a copy. Contiguous inputs and inputs
with compatible strides can be reshaped without copying, but you should not
depend on the copying vs. viewing behavior. 

See [`torch.Tensor.view()`](torch.Tensor.view.html#torch.Tensor.view "torch.Tensor.view")  on when it is possible to return a view. 

A single dimension may be -1, in which case it’s inferred from the remaining
dimensions and the number of elements in `input`  . 

Parameters
:   * **input** ( [*Tensor*](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor")  ) – the tensor to be reshaped
* **shape** ( [*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#tuple "(in Python v3.13)") *of* [*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#int "(in Python v3.13)")  ) – the new shape

Example: 

```
>>> a = torch.arange(4.)
>>> torch.reshape(a, (2, 2))
tensor([[ 0.,  1.],
        [ 2.,  3.]])
>>> b = torch.tensor([[0, 1], [2, 3]])
>>> torch.reshape(b, (-1,))
tensor([ 0,  1,  2,  3])

```

>>> handle.remove() # Removes the hook
>>> a.grad = None
>>> b.sum().backward(retain_graph=True)
>>> print(a.grad)

Let's start with a general discussion of how PyTorch frees memory:

First, we should emphasize that PyTorch uses an implicitly declared graph that is stored in Python object attributes. (Remember, it's Python, so everything is an object). More specifically, torch.autograd.Variables have a .grad_fn attribute. This attribute's type defines what kind of computation node we have (e.g. an addition), and the input to that node.

This is important because Pytorch frees memory simply by using the standard python garbage collector (if fairly aggressively). In this context, this means that the (implicitly declared) computation graphs will be kept alive as long as there are references to the objects holding them in the current scope!

This means that if you e.g. do some kind of batching on samples s_1 ... s_k, compute the loss for each and add the loss at the end, that cumulative loss will hold references to each individual loss, which in turn holds references to each of the computation nodes that computed it.

So your question applied to your code is more about how Python (or, more specifically its garbage collector) handles references than about Pytorch does. Since you accumulate the loss in one object (total_loss), you keep pointers alive, and thereby do not free the memory until you re-initialize that object in the outer loop.

Applied to your example, this means that the computation graph you create in the forward pass (at out = model(im)) is only referenced by the out object and any future computations thereof. So if you compute the loss and sum it, you will keep references to out alive, and thereby to the computation graph. If you do not use it, however, the garbage collector should recursively collect out, and its computation graph.

===========================================================================

At the heart of PyTorch data loading utility is the [`torch.utils.data.DataLoader`](#torch.utils.data.DataLoader "torch.utils.data.DataLoader")  class. It represents a Python iterable over a dataset, with support for 

* [map-style and iterable-style datasets](#dataset-types)  ,
* [customizing data loading order](#data-loading-order-and-sampler)  ,
* [automatic batching](#loading-batched-and-non-batched-data)  ,
* [single- and multi-process data loading](#single-and-multi-process-data-loading)  ,
* [automatic memory pinning](#memory-pinning)  .

These options are configured by the constructor arguments of a [`DataLoader`](#torch.utils.data.DataLoader "torch.utils.data.DataLoader")  , which has signature: 

```
DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=1, shuffle=False, sampler=None,
           batch_sampler=None, num_workers=0, collate_fn=None,
           pin_memory=False, drop_last=False, timeout=0,
           worker_init_fn=None, *, prefetch_factor=2,
           persistent_workers=False)

```

The sections below describe in details the effects and usages of these options. 

Dataset Types 
--------------------------------------------------------------

The most important argument of [`DataLoader`](#torch.utils.data.DataLoader "torch.utils.data.DataLoader")  constructor is [`dataset`](utils.html#module-torch.utils.data.dataset "torch.utils.data.dataset")  , which indicates a dataset object to load data
from. PyTorch supports two different types of datasets:

---

### Single-process data loading (default) 

In this mode, data fetching is done in the same process a [`DataLoader`](#torch.utils.data.DataLoader "torch.utils.data.DataLoader")  is initialized. Therefore, data loading
may block computing. However, this mode may be preferred when resource(s) used
for sharing data among processes (e.g., shared memory, file descriptors) is
limited, or when the entire dataset is small and can be loaded entirely in
memory. Additionally, single-process loading often shows more readable error
traces and thus is useful for debugging.

The `CyclicLR` is not changing the learning rate of your optimizer. It's just updating the value of `lr` for each parameter group.

When you call `scheduler.step()`, it updates the values of `lr` for each parameter group with the new value calculated by the scheduler. This doesn't change the actual learning rate used by the optimizer. The optimizer uses the value of `lr` from the parameter groups when calling `.step()` on it.

So, if you want to see what the current learning rate is, you can do:

```
for param_group in optimizer.param_groups:
    print(param_group['lr'])
```

Note that you'll probably need to change some other things as well, depending on your specific task.

The `pretrained` flag only affects the mask head, which you don't want to use anyway.

If you set `pretrained=False`, then you will get a new backbone (resnet50) with random weights. If you set it to `True`, then you'll get the same backbone as if you had trained from scratch, but with pre-trained weights. This means that your network will start off with some knowledge about images, so training will take less time.

As for the other two flags:

- `pretrained_backbone`: whether or not to load pretrained weights for the backbone.
- `trainable_backbone_layers`: how many layers of the backbone to train. If you set it to 3, then only the last three layers of the resnet will be trained. If you set it to 1, then only the last layer will be trained. Setting it to None means that all layers will be trained.

So, if you want to train from scratch, you can set them both to False. If you want to continue training from a checkpoint, you can set them both to True. If you want to fine-tune the backbone, you can set one of them to True and the other to False.

The problem here is that you're creating your `hidden_layers` list before calling `super().__init__`, which means that the `nn.Module` constructor will not be able to register any of those modules.

To fix this, you need to move the creation of the `hidden_layers` list inside the `__init__` method after calling `super().__init__`. This ensures that the `nn.Module` constructor gets called first, so that it can properly register the `hidden_layers` modules.

Batch Normalization layer has different behavior in training vs. inferencing:

  1. During training (i.e. when using fit() or when calling the layer/model with the argument training=True), the layer normalizes its output using the mean and standard deviation of the current batch of inputs.

  2. During inference (i.e. when using evaluate() or predict() or when calling the layer/model with the argument training=False (which is the default), the layer normalizes its output using a moving average of the mean and standard deviation of the batches it has seen during training.

So, the first result is due to default training=False and the second is due to default is_training=True.

The difference comes from the fact that `BatchNorm` in Keras and TensorFlow has two modes: training mode and inference mode.
In training mode, it uses the mean and variance computed on the current batch, while in inference mode it uses the running average of the mean and variance.

By default, `BatchNorm` in Keras is set to training mode, so you get the first output.
If you switch to inference mode by setting `training=False`, you will get the second output:

```
import tensorflow as tf

bn = tf.keras.layers.BatchNormalization()
x = tf.convert_to_tensor([[5.0, 70.0], [5.0, 60.0]])
print(bn(x)) # Training mode
print(bn(x, training=False)) # Inference mode
```

First you need to understand the ranks. To be brief: in a multiprocessing context we typically assume that rank 0 is the first process or base process. The other processes are then ranked differently, e.g. 1, 2, 3, totalling four processes in total.

Some operations are not necessary to be done in parallel or you just need one process to do some preprocessing or caching so that the other processes can use that data.

In your example, if the first if statement is entered by the non-base processes (rank 1, 2, 3), they will block (or "wait") because they run into the barrier. They wait there, because barrier() blocks until all processes have reached a barrier, but the base process has not reached a barrier yet.

So at this point the non-base processes (1, 2, 3) are blocked, but the base process (0) continues. The base process will do some operations (preprocess and cache data, in this case) until it reaches the second if-statement. There, the base process will run into a barrier. At this point, all processes have stopped at a barrier, meaning that all current barriers can be lifted and all processes can continue. Because the base process prepared the data, the other processes can now use that data.

Perhaps the most important thing to understand is:

  • when a process encounters a barrier it will block
  • the position of the barrier is not important (not all processes have to enter the same if-statement, for instance)
  • a process is blocked by a barrier until all processes have encountered a barrier, upon which those barriers are lifted for all processes

The barrier is there to ensure that all workers have finished their tasks before proceeding with the next one.

In your example, the first barrier ensures that all workers have finished preprocessing the data before any worker starts saving the preprocessed data. The second barrier ensures that all workers have finished loading the model and the vocabulary before any worker starts using them.

This is necessary because the model and the vocabulary need to be loaded by all workers before they can start using them. If one worker started using the model and the vocabulary before the other workers had finished loading them, it would lead to errors.

The reason why the second barrier is only checked for `local_rank == 0` is because the model and the vocabulary only need to be loaded once per node. All workers on the same node will share the same model and vocabulary, so they don't need to load them multiple times. Only the worker with `local_rank == 0` needs to load the model and the vocabulary, and then the barrier ensures that all other workers have finished loading them as well.

For backward compatibility, it may be necessary for users to handle both
cases in their argument parsing code. This means including both `"--local-rank"`  and `"--local_rank"`  in the argument parser. If only `"--local_rank"`  is
provided, the launcher will trigger an error: “error: unrecognized arguments:
–local-rank=<rank>”. For training code that only supports PyTorch 2.0.0+,
including `"--local-rank"`  should be sufficient.

I think you're confusing two different concepts:

* **Feature extraction**: This is what you do when you use a pretrained network for inference on new data. You take the pretrained network, remove the final layer(s), and use the rest of the network to get features for your new data.
* **Clustering**: This is a completely separate task where you try to group similar data points together.

The first step is not related to clustering at all. The second step is not related to feature extraction at all. They are two completely different things.

If you want to cluster your data, you can just train a simple neural network with a single linear layer on top of the pretrained network. Then you can use this network to predict the cluster labels for your data. If you want to visualize the clusters, you can use t-SNE or PCA to reduce the dimensionality of the features before plotting them.

The `Trainer` class is a wrapper around the `DataLoader`, `model`, `optimizer`, `loss function` and `metric`. The `Trainer` class takes care of all the training loop, evaluation loop, saving/loading checkpoints, etc.

In your case, you have two classes:

```
class InputFeature:
    def __init__(self, text, label):
        self.input_ids = text
        self.label = label
```

and

```
class InputFeaturePlural:
    def __init__(self, text, label):
        self.input_ids = text
        self.labels = label
```

The first one will be used when you pass the `train_dataset` to the `Trainer` class. The second one will be used when you pass the `eval_dataset` to the `Trainer` class.

This is because the `Trainer` class has two methods: `create_optimizer_and_scheduler` and `compute_metrics`.

The first one is called when you call the `train` method of the `Trainer` class. In this method, the `Trainer` class calls the `DataLoader`'s `__iter__` method. This method returns an iterator that yields batches of data. Each batch is a list of `InputFeature` objects. The `Trainer` class then passes each batch to the `model`'s `forward` method. The `forward` method expects a list of `InputFeature` objects and returns a tuple containing the loss and the predictions.

The second one is called when you call the `evaluate` method of the `Trainer` class. In this method, the `Trainer` class calls the `DataLoader`'s `__iter__` method. This method returns an iterator that yields batches of data. Each batch is a list of `InputFeaturePlural` objects. The `Trainer` class then passes each batch to the `model`'s `forward` method. The `forward` method expects a list of `InputFeaturePlural` objects and returns a tuple containing the loss and the predictions.

So, the `Trainer` class is responsible for converting the `train_dataset` and `eval_dataset` into batches of data. The `Trainer` class is also responsible for calling the `model`'s `forward` method and computing the loss and the predictions. The `Trainer` class is also responsible for calling the `optimizer`'s `step` method and updating the weights of the `model`. The `Trainer` class is also responsible for calling the `scheduler`'s `step` method and updating the learning rate of the `optimizer`. The `Trainer` class is also responsible for calling the `compute_metrics` method and computing the metrics.

I think you're misunderstanding what `torch.bool` does.

In particular, `x *= y` will only work as expected when `y` is a tensor with the same shape as `x`, containing only `True` or `False`. If `y` is a scalar boolean value, then it will just multiply `x` by `1` or `0`.

def forward(self, x):
    # Only one gate is supposed to be enabled at random
    # However, for the experiment, I fixed the values to [1,0] and [1,1]
    choice  =  randint(0,1)
    gate_A  =  torch.tensor([choice]*16, dtype=torch.bool) 
    gate_B  =  torch.tensor([1-choice]*16, dtype=torch.bool) 

    a = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv1a(x)))
    a = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv2a(a)))

    b = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv1b(x)))
    b = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv2b(b)))

    a *= gate_A
    b *= gate_B
    x  = torch.cat( [a,b], dim = 1 )

    x = torch.flatten(x, 1) # flatten all dimensions except batch
    x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
    x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
    x = self.fc3(x)
    return x

The first version is correct.

`zero_grad()` clears out the gradients computed from the last step. Otherwise they would accumulate between batches and give you wrong results.

The default behavior (letting `.grad`  s be `None`  before the first `backward()`  , such that their layout is created according to 1 or 2,
and retained over time according to 3 or 4) is recommended for best performance.
Calls to `model.zero_grad()`  or `optimizer.zero_grad()`  will not affect `.grad`  layouts. 

In fact, resetting all `.grad`  s to `None`  before each
accumulation phase, e.g.: 

```
for iterations...
    ...
    for param in model.parameters():
        param.grad = None
    loss.backward()

```

such that they’re recreated according to 1 or 2 every time,
is a valid alternative to `model.zero_grad()`  or `optimizer.zero_grad()`  that may improve performance for some networks.

The `DefaultPredictor` returns a dictionary containing several fields including `instances`, which contains all the predictions.

In particular, `instances.pred_masks` is a tensor of shape `(N, H, W)` where `N` is the number of instances, `H` is the height of the image and `W` is the width of the image. Each element of the tensor is a binary mask indicating whether a pixel belongs to an instance or not.

To get the coordinates of the pixels belonging to an instance, you can simply iterate over the elements of the tensor and keep track of the indices of the elements that are equal to 1. This can be done using NumPy's `np.where()` function:

```

:   Prune tensor corresponding to parameter called `name`  in `module`  by applying the pre-computed mask in `mask`  . 

Modifies module in place (and also return the modified module) by: 

1. adding a named buffer called `name+'_mask'`  corresponding to the
binary mask applied to the parameter `name`  by the pruning method.
2. replacing the parameter `name`  by its pruned version, while the
original (unpruned) parameter is stored in a new parameter named `name+'_orig'`  .

will act.
* **mask** ( [*Tensor*](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor")  ) – binary mask to be applied to the parameter.

Discriminator's job is to perform Binary Classification to detect between Real and Fake so its loss function is Binary Cross Entropy.

What Generator does is Density Estimation, from the noise to real data, and feed it to Discriminator to fool it.

The approach followed in the design is to model it as MinMax game. Now let's have a look at cost functions:

Someone explained this as:

The first term in J(D) represents feeding the actual data to the discriminator, and the discriminator would want to maximize the log probability of predicting one, indicating that the data is real. The second term represents the samples generated by G. Here, the discriminator would want to maximize the log probability of predicting zero, indicating the the data is fake. The generator, on the other hand tries to minimize the log probability of the discriminator being correct. The solution to this problem is an equilibrium point of the game, which is a saddle point of the discriminator loss.

Since the Discriminator tries to maximize the probability of Generator's sample as Zero, the Generator's job becomes to maximize for one. This is equivalent to making the Generator’s cost function the negative cross entropy, where the first term in J(D) would now be constant.

The first equation you posted is the mathematical formulation of the generator's objective function.

In this case, the generator tries to minimize the cross-entropy loss between its generated samples and real samples. The generator does not know what the real samples look like, so it cannot directly compute the cross-entropy loss. Instead, it tries to fool the discriminator into thinking that its generated samples are real. If the discriminator is fooled, then the generator has successfully minimized the cross-entropy loss.

The second piece of code you posted is the implementation of the generator's objective function in PyTorch. In this case, the generator tries to maximize the probability that the discriminator outputs a real label for its generated samples. This is equivalent to minimizing the cross-entropy loss between the discriminator's output and the real label.

### Division by Zero in Autograd 

When performing division by zero in PyTorch (e.g., `x / 0`  ), the forward pass will produce `inf`  values following IEEE-754 floating point arithmetic. While these `inf`  values can be masked out before computing the final loss (e.g., via indexing or masking), the autograd system still tracks and differentiates through the full computation graph, including the division by zero operation. 

During backpropagation, this can lead to problematic gradient expressions. For example: 

```
x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

y = x / div          # Results in [inf, 1]
mask = div != 0      # [False, True]
loss = y[mask].sum()
loss.backward()
print(x.grad)        # [nan, 1], not [0, 1]

```

In this example, even though we only use the masked output (which excludes the division by zero), autograd still computes gradients through the full computation graph, including the division by zero operation. This results in `nan`  gradients for the masked elements, which can cause training instability. 

To avoid this issue, there are several recommended approaches: 

1. Mask before division:

```
x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

mask = div != 0
safe = torch.zeros_like(x)
safe[mask] = x[mask] / div[mask]
loss = safe.sum()
loss.backward()      # Produces safe gradients [0, 1]

```

2. Use MaskedTensor (experimental API):

```
from torch.masked import as_masked_tensor

x = torch.tensor([1., 1.], requires_grad=True)
div = torch.tensor([0., 1.])

The returned tensor and buffer share the same memory. Modifications to
the tensor will be reflected in the buffer and vice versa. The returned
tensor is not resizable.

owns the shared memory. Therefore, such memory will not be deallocated

In short, it's a way to train your network progressively harder over time. You start with a low dropout rate (e.g. 0.1), then gradually increase it until you reach the desired value (e.g. 0.5).

Here is an example implementation:

```
import torch.nn as nn

class CurricularDropout(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, p=0.5, schedule=None):
        super().__init__()
        self.p = p
        self.schedule = schedule or lambda x: x

    def forward(self, input):
        if self.training:
            mask = input.new().resize_as_(input)
            mask.bernoulli_(self.schedule(self.p))
            return input * mask / self.p
        else:
            return input

CPU in multiprocessing 
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Inappropriate multiprocessing can lead to CPU oversubscription, causing
different processes to compete for CPU resources, resulting in low
efficiency. 

This tutorial will explain what CPU oversubscription is and how to
avoid it.

---

Examples::

>>> import numpy as np
>>>

>>>     return torch.from_numpy(y_np)

I've looked a bit into this tonight. I don't have a solution (edit: I have a mitigation, see the edit at end), but I have a bit more information.

It seems the issue is caused by NVidia fatbins (.nv_fatb) being loaded into memory. Several DLLs, such as cusolver64_xx.dll, torcha_cuda_cu.dll, and a few others, have .nv_fatb sections in them. These contain tons of different variations of CUDA code for different GPUs, so it ends up being several hundred megabytes to a couple gigabytes.

When Python imports 'torch' it loads these DLLs, and maps the .nv_fatb section into memory. For some reason, instead of just being a memory mapped file, it is actually taking up memory. The section is set as 'copy on write', so it's possible something writes into it? I don't know. But anyway, if you look at Python using VMMap ( https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/vmmap ) you can see that these DLLs are committing huge amounts of committed memory for this .nv_fatb section. The frustrating part is it doesn't seem to be using the memory. For example, right now my Python.exe has 2.7GB committed, but the working set is only 148MB.

Every Python process that loads these DLLs will commit several GB of memory loading these DLLs. So if 1 Python process is wasting 2GB of memory, and you try running 8 workers, you need 16GB of memory to spare just to load the DLLs. It really doesn't seem like this memory is used, just committed.

I don't know enough about these fatbinaries to try to fix it, but from looking at this for the past 2 hours it really seems like they are the issue. Perhaps its an NVidia problem that these are committing memory?

edit: I made this python script: https://gist.github.com/cobryan05/7d1fe28dd370e110a372c4d268dcb2e5

Get it and install its pefile dependency ( python -m pip install pefile ).

Run it on your torch and cuda DLLs. In OPs case, command line might look like:

python fixNvPe.py --input=C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python38\lib\site-packages\torch\lib\*.dll

(You also want to run this wherever your cusolver64_*.dll and friends are. This may be in your torch\lib folder, or it may be, eg, C:\Program Files\NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit\CUDA\vXX.X\bin . If it is under Program Files, you will need to run the script with administrative privileges)

What this script is going to do is scan through all DLLs specified by the input glob, and if it finds an .nv_fatb section it will back up the DLL, disable ASLR, and mark the .nv_fatb section read-only.

ASLR is 'address space layout randomization.' It is a security feature that randomizes where a DLL is loaded in memory. We disable it for this DLL so that all Python processes will load the DLL into the same base virtual address. If all Python processes using the DLL load it at the same base address, they can all share the DLL. Otherwise each process needs its own copy.

Marking the section 'read-only' lets Windows know that the contents will not change in memory. If you map a file into memory read/write, Windows has to commit enough memory, backed by the pagefile, just in case you make a modification to it. If the section is read-only, there is no need to back it in the pagefile. We know there are no modifications to it, so it can always be found in the DLL.

The theory behind the script is that by changing these 2 flags that less memory will be committed for the .nv_fatb, and more memory will be shared between the Python processes. In practice, it works. Not quite as well as I'd hope (it still commits a lot more than it uses), so my understanding may be flawed, but it significantly decreases memory commit.

In my limited testing I haven't ran into any issues, but I can't guarantee there are no code paths that attempts to write to that section we marked 'read only.' If you start running into issues, though, you can just restore the backups.

edit 2022-01-20: Per NVIDIA: "We have gone ahead and marked the nv_fatb section as read-only, this change will be targeting next major CUDA release 11.7 . We are not changing the ASLR, as that is considered a safety feature ."

This should certainly help. If it's not enough without ASLR as well then the script should still work

**TLDR:** You need to increase your system's virtual memory size.

---

When you start a new process, Python will load all the modules and their dependencies into memory. This includes `torch` and all its dependencies. If you're running 50 processes, then you'll need enough space to hold 50 copies of these modules.

In Windows, the default virtual memory size is 2 GB. This means that if you're trying to load 50 copies of `torch`, you'll need 10 GB of free memory. Since you only have 8 GB of RAM, you'll need to increase your virtual memory size.

To do this:

- Right click on **Computer**
- Click on **Properties**
- Click on **Advanced System Settings**
- Click on **Performance**
- Click on **Settings**
- Click on **Advanced**
- Click on **Change**
- Increase the **Initial Size** and **Maximum Size** values to something larger than 8 GB (e.g., 16 GB)

Now you should be able to run 50 processes without any issues.

### Combined or separate [`forward()`](../generated/torch.autograd.Function.forward.html#torch.autograd.Function.forward "torch.autograd.Function.forward")  and `setup_context()` 

There are two main ways to define [`Function`](../autograd.html#torch.autograd.Function "torch.autograd.Function")  . Either: 

* define a [`forward()`](../generated/torch.autograd.Function.forward.html#torch.autograd.Function.forward "torch.autograd.Function.forward")  that combines the forward compute logic with `setup_context()`
* (as of PyTorch 2.0) define a separate [`forward()`](../generated/torch.autograd.Function.forward.html#torch.autograd.Function.forward "torch.autograd.Function.forward")  and `setup_context()`

We recommend the second option (separate [`forward()`](../generated/torch.autograd.Function.forward.html#torch.autograd.Function.forward "torch.autograd.Function.forward")  and `setup_context()`  )
because that is closer to how PyTorch native operations are implemented and it composes
with [`torch.func`](../func.api.html#module-torch.func "torch.func")  transforms. However, we plan to support both approaches going forward;
combining [`forward()`](../generated/torch.autograd.Function.forward.html#torch.autograd.Function.forward "torch.autograd.Function.forward")  with `setup_context()`  : leads to more flexibility since
you are able to save intermediates without returning them as output.

---

### [Functions with multiple inputs or autocastable ops](#id14) 

Apply [`custom_fwd`](../amp.html#torch.amp.custom_fwd "torch.amp.custom_fwd")  and [`custom_bwd`](../amp.html#torch.amp.custom_bwd "torch.amp.custom_bwd")  (with no arguments) to `forward`  and `backward`  respectively. These ensure `forward`  executes with the current autocast state and `backward`  executes with the same autocast state as `forward`  (which can prevent type mismatch errors): 

```
class MyMM(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    @custom_fwd
    def forward(ctx, a, b):
        ctx.save_for_backward(a, b)
        return a.mm(b)
    @staticmethod
    @custom_bwd
    def backward(ctx, grad):
        a, b = ctx.saved_tensors
        return grad.mm(b.t()), a.t().mm(grad)

```

Now `MyMM`  can be invoked anywhere, without disabling autocast or manually casting inputs: 

```
mymm = MyMM.apply

with autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.float16):
    output = mymm(input1, input2)

```

So basically, you have a sequence of characters and you want to predict the correct sequence of characters. For example, let's assume you have a sequence of characters like "hello world". Now, you want to predict the correct sequence of characters. So, you would have something like this:

```
input = torch.rand((seq_len, batch_size, num_classes))

Now, you can compute the loss using CTCLoss.

The `reduction` argument of [`F.cross_entropy`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy.html#torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy) is used to specify what should be done with the losses computed for each element of the batch.

- `'none'`: no reduction will be applied, i.e., the output is simply the loss per sample.
- `'mean'`: the mean of the individual losses is taken.
- `'sum'`: the output will be summed.

In your case, you want to compute the average loss over the entire dataset, so you need to sum up the losses for each sample and then divide by the number of samples:

total_loss += loss.item() * len(images)

nn.DataParallel wraps the model, where the actual model is assigned to the module attribute. That also means that the keys in the state dict have a module. prefix.

Let's look at a very simplified version with just one convolution to see the difference:

The state dict you saved with nn.DataParallel does not line up with the regular model's state. You are merging the current state dict with the loaded state dict, that means that the loaded state is ignored, because the model does not have any attributes that belong to the keys and instead you are left with the randomly initialised model.

To avoid making that mistake, you shouldn't merge the state dicts, but rather directly apply it to the model, in which case there will be an error if the keys don't match.

I think you have misunderstood how `DataParallel` works.

When you do

```
model = nn.DataParallel(model, device_ids=device_ids)
```

you're telling Pytorch that your model should be replicated across all GPUs specified by `device_ids`. This means that each of these GPUs will receive a copy of the model and perform computations independently. The outputs from each of these copies will then be combined into one final output (which is what you want).

However, this does not mean that the parameters of the model will be shared between the different copies. In fact, it's the opposite - each copy has its own set of parameters. When you call `model.parameters()` or `model.named_parameters()`, you'll see that there are as many sets of parameters as there are copies of the model.

So, when you load the weights using

```
model.load_state_dict(torch.load('path_to_weights'))
```

Pytorch will try to match the names of the parameters in the loaded state dict with those in the model. Since the names don't match (because they belong to different copies), nothing will happen.

To fix this, you need to make sure that the names of the parameters in the loaded state dict match those in the model. You can do this by either:

- Loading the weights directly onto the desired device (e.g., `cuda(0)`).
- Using [`load_state_dict`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/nn.html#torch.nn.Module.load_state_dict) with the `strict=False` option.
- Manually renaming the keys in the state dict before loading them.

The embedding layer is not supposed to change during training. It's just a lookup table that maps each token id to its corresponding vector.

If you want to use a pretrained embedding, you can initialize your embedding layer with it:

```
embedding = torch.nn.Embedding(num_embeddings, embedding_dim)
embedding.weight.data.copy_(pretrained_embedding)
```

Then, if you don't want to update this embedding during training, you can set `requires_grad` to False:

embedding.weight.requires_grad = False

Similar to NumPy you can insert a singleton dimension ("unsqueeze" a dimension) by indexing this dimension with None. In turn n[:, None] will have the effect of inserting a new dimension on dim=1. This is equivalent to n.unsqueeze(dim=1):

>>> n = torch.rand(3, 100, 100)

>>> n[:, None].shape
(3, 1, 100, 100)

>>> n.unsqueeze(1).shape
(3, 1, 100, 100)

Here are some other types of None indexings.

In the example above : is was used as a placeholder to designate the first dimension dim=0. If you want to insert a dimension on dim=2, you can add a second : as n[:, :, None].

You can also place None with respect to the last dimension instead. To do so you can use the ellipsis syntax ...:

  • n[..., None] will insert a dimension last, i.e. n.unsqueeze(dim=-1).

  • n[..., None, :] on the before last dimension, i.e. n.unsqueeze(dim=-2).

The `None` keyword is used to add an extra dimension to your tensor.
In particular, `n[:, None]` will create a new dimension at the second position (index 1) of `n`. This is equivalent to calling `n.unsqueeze(1)`.

For example:

```
>>> n = torch.tensor([1,2,3])
>>> n.shape
torch.Size([3])

>>> n[:, None]
tensor([[1],
        [2],
        [3]])

>>> n[:, None].shape
torch.Size([3, 1])
```

Your network is not learning because your loss function is wrong.

In your case, you have a binary classification problem, so you should use `torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss` instead of `torch.nn.MSELoss`. The reason why this works is that `BCEWithLogitsLoss` applies sigmoid activation on its input before computing the loss. This means that if the predicted value is close enough to 0 or 1, the loss will be small even if the prediction is not perfect. On the other hand, `MSELoss` does not apply any activation function, so the loss will be large if the prediction is far from 0 or 1.

I'm not familiar with A2C but I can answer your questions about how gradient computation works in general.
In order to compute the gradients of some function `f` w.r.t. its inputs you need to define it as a [`torch.autograd.Function`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/autograd.html#torch.autograd.Function) (or use one of the built-in functions). Then you can call `backward()` on an output tensor of `f`, which will compute the gradients for all tensors that have `requires_grad=True`. The gradients will be stored in the `.grad` attribute of each such tensor.

For example:

```
import torch

class MyFunction(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x):
        return x * 2

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        # This is where we compute the gradients of the output w.r.t. the input.
        # Note that the gradients of `ctx.input0` should accumulate,
        # i.e. if the value "use" of our function results in
        # gradients w.r.t. the same node, then those gradients should
        # be added up, not replaced.
        ctx.save_for_backward(grad_output)
        return grad_output * 2

x = torch.tensor([1., 2., 3.], requires_grad=True)
y = MyFunction.apply(x)

# Compute gradients of y w.r.t. x
y.backward()
print(x.grad)  # [2., 4., 6.]

# Alternatively:
with torch.enable_grad():
    z = x * 2
z.backward()
print(x.grad)  # [2., 4., 6.]
```

I think you're misinterpreting the results.

Firstly, let's look at the analytical solution:

```
import numpy as np

true = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]])
pred = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]])

loss_analytical = -np.sum(true*np.log(pred))/pred.shape[0]
print(loss_analytical)
# nan
```

This gives `nan` because we're taking the logarithm of zero. This is not surprising since our predictions are identical to our targets.

Now, let's look at the TensorFlow solution:

```
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import backend as K

loss = tf.keras.losses.CategoricalCrossentropy()

loss(pred, true).numpy()
# 8.05904769897461
```

We get a different answer because TensorFlow uses numerical stability tricks to avoid underflow. Specifically, they subtract the maximum value before exponentiating:

```
def safe_log(x):
    return K.log(x + K.epsilon())

def safe_exp(x):
    return K.exp(x - K.max(x))

safe_loss = -tf.reduce_mean(
    true * safe_log(safe_exp(pred - K.max(pred)))
)

safe_loss.numpy()
# 8.05904769897461
```

So, both solutions give the same answer. The difference is that TensorFlow avoids underflow by using these tricks.

The problem seems to be that you're not interpolating correctly between your input ranges.

If you have an input value `x` in the range `[min_in, max_in]`, then you can interpolate it to a value `y` in the range `[min_out, max_out]` by doing:

```
y = min_out + (max_out - min_out) * ((x - min_in) / (max_in - min_in))
```

In your case, you have `min_in = -1`, `max_in = 1`, `min_out = -128`, and `max_out = 127`. So you get:

```
y = -128 + (127 - (-128)) * ((x - (-1)) / (1 - (-1)))
  = -128 + 255 * ((x + 1) / 2)
  = -128 + 127 * (x + 1)
  = -128 + 127*x + 127
  = 127*x - 1
```

So your code should look something like this:

```
def map_l(x):
    return 127*x - 1

def map_ab(x):
    return 127*x
```

The key principle is to prevent the division by zero operation from being recorded in the computation graph, rather than masking its results after the fact. This ensures that autograd only computes gradients through valid operations. 

This behavior is important to keep in mind when working with operations that might produce `inf`  or `nan`  values, as masking the outputs does not prevent the problematic gradients from being computed.

Locally disabling gradient computation 
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

There are several mechanisms available from Python to locally disable gradient
computation: 

To disable gradients across entire blocks of code, there are context managers
like no-grad mode and inference mode.
For more fine-grained exclusion of subgraphs from gradient computation,
there is setting the `requires_grad`  field of a tensor. 

Below, in addition to discussing the mechanisms above, we also describe
evaluation mode ( `nn.Module.eval()`  ), a method that is not used
to disable gradient computation but, because of its name, is often mixed up with the three.

---

Examples::
:   ```
>>> class Inplace(Function):
>>>     @staticmethod
>>>     def forward(ctx, x):
>>>         x_npy = x.numpy() # x_npy shares storage with x
>>>         x_npy += 1
>>>         ctx.mark_dirty(x)
>>>         return x
>>>
>>>     @staticmethod
>>>     @once_differentiable
>>>     def backward(ctx, grad_output):
>>>         return grad_output
>>>
>>> a = torch.tensor(1., requires_grad=True, dtype=torch.double).clone()

>>>                   # but the engine would not know unless we mark_dirty
>>> b.backward() # RuntimeError: one of the variables needed for gradient
>>>              # computation has been modified by an inplace operation

```

The targets are treated as samples from Gaussian distributions with
expectations and variances predicted by the neural network. For a `target`  tensor modelled as having Gaussian distribution with a tensor
of expectations `input`  and a tensor of positive variances `var`  the loss is:

>>> input = torch.randn(5, 2, requires_grad=True)

>>> input = torch.randn(5, 2, requires_grad=True)

gradients are unaffected by it.

CrossEntropyLoss 
====================================================================

*class* torch.nn. CrossEntropyLoss ( *weight = None*  , *size_average = None*  , *ignore_index = -100*  , *reduce = None*  , *reduction = 'mean'*  , *label_smoothing = 0.0* ) [source](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.8.0/torch/nn/modules/loss.py#L1158) 
:   This criterion computes the cross entropy loss between input logits
and target. 

It is useful when training a classification problem with *C* classes.
If provided, the optional argument `weight`  should be a 1D *Tensor* assigning weight to each of the classes.
This is particularly useful when you have an unbalanced training set.
